common_name: Rosa di Gorizia Radicchio (Gorizia Rose Radicchio)

planting.note: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a late-fall and winter harvest; the rosette only forms its namesake shape and loses bitterness after repeated hard frosts, so growers in the variety's native Friuli-Venezia Giulia traditionally dig and trim roots after freezing weather, then force new pale growth in cellars or covered beds through winter.

directions: Rosa di Gorizia is a prized open, loose-rosette radicchio from the countryside around Gorizia in Friuli-Venezia Giulia, forming elongated pink-and-cream leaves with white ribs that fan outward into a shape resembling a rose once cold weather arrives. Unlike closed-head radicchio types, plants are often lifted after the first hard frosts, trimmed of outer leaves and roots, and set in sand in a cool cellar or cold frame to blanch and sweeten further before the final winter harvest. Give plants a long, cool growing season and avoid rushing summer sowings, since heat keeps the rosette green and bitter. Harvest after repeated freezes for the sweetest flavor and most vivid rose coloring.

common_name: Variegato di Lusia Radicchio (Lusia IGP Radicchio)

planting.note: Sow in mid-to-late summer for an autumn and early-winter crop, since cool nights are needed to trigger the characteristic red-and-cream variegation and to firm up the loosely folded heads.

directions: Variegato di Lusia carries Protected Geographical Indication (IGP) status for the Rovigo-province town of Lusia in the Veneto, where it is grown in the sandy alluvial soils of the Adige river valley. Heads are loosely folded rather than tightly closed, with crisp cream-colored leaves marbled and streaked in deep wine-red, a pattern that intensifies as autumn nights cool. The flavor is milder and less bitter than many red radicchio types, making it popular both raw in salads and lightly grilled. Sow in summer for fall harvest and avoid waterlogged soil, which the variety's sandy native ground does not replicate well.

common_name: Fagiolo del Purgatorio Bean (Purgatory Bean, Gradoli Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; this is a compact bush type, so no poles or trellis are needed.

directions: Fagiolo del Purgatorio is a small, thin-skinned white heirloom bean traditionally grown around Gradoli on the shores of Lake Bolsena in Lazio, where it takes its name from the Lenten custom of eating the beans, plain and unadorned, as a form of penance in the weeks before Easter. The tiny, nearly translucent-skinned seeds cook quickly to a smooth, creamy texture without an overnight soak. Grow as a compact bush bean with no staking required, and harvest pods once they have dried and rattle on the plant. Thresh and cure the beans a further week indoors before sealing them away for storage.
sources: Region of Lazio agricultural heritage crop records

common_name: Fagiolo di Sarconi Bean (Sarconi Bean, Val d'Agri IGP Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably warm; provide poles or a trellis, as plants climb vigorously in the irrigated valley fields of the Val d'Agri where the variety is traditionally grown.

directions: Fagiolo di Sarconi carries Protected Geographical Indication (IGP) status for the Val d'Agri valley around Sarconi in Basilicata, where several traditional bean types — including cannellino, borlotto, and fagiolino forms — are grown together under the single collective name. The variety is known for thin skins and a creamy, evenly cooking interior prized in regional soups and stews. Provide a tall pole or trellis for the vigorous climbing vines and consistent irrigation through pod fill, mirroring the valley's irrigated fields. Let pods dry fully on the vine before shelling, then cure the beans indoors for a week before storing airtight.
sources: Region of Basilicata agricultural heritage crop records

common_name: Cannellino di Atina Bean (Atina DOP White Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; provide poles or a trellis, since the variety is a vigorous climbing type traditionally grown along the Melfa and Mollarino river valleys near Atina.

directions: Cannellino di Atina holds Protected Designation of Origin (DOP) status for the river valleys around Atina in southern Lazio, where mineral-rich alluvial soil and clean valley water are credited with the bean's thin skin and especially smooth, buttery texture once cooked. The slender white seeds are larger and more elongated than ordinary cannellini beans. Give vines a tall pole or trellis and even moisture through pod fill, then allow pods to dry completely before shelling. Cure the harvested beans indoors for a week or two before sealing them away for winter storage.
sources: Region of Lazio agricultural heritage crop records
